title: Can a hundred kilometres a day reach the Moon in ten years?
description: Ruhee travels a hundred kilometres every day towards the Moon. The distance is found in stages, first for a year and then for ten years, and set beside the distance to the Moon. Keeko raises the doubt that a hundred times three hundred sixty five has only one zero.
teaching_notes: One idea: find a big distance in stages, a year first and then ten years, and compare it with the target. Watch for students who write only one zero when multiplying by a hundred.

source: If I could travel 100 kilometres every day, could I reach the Moon in 10 years? (The distance between the Earth and the Moon is 3,84,400 km.) How far would she have travelled in a year? How far would she have travelled in 10 years?
video_script.why: The child can multiply large numbers and now uses stages to judge whether a long journey reaches its target.
video_script.substitution: Distance is the distance in one day times the number of days; find one year first, then ten years, then compare with the target.
video_script.anchor: a traveller on a road, the Moon far above, and the distance 3,84,400 km
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko writes only one zero after 365 when multiplying by a hundred, so a year comes out as 3,650 km instead of 36,500 km.
video_script.payoff_line: Ruhee falls short of the Moon by nineteen thousand four hundred kilometres

final_answer.value: 36,500 km in a year; 3,65,000 km in 10 years; 19,400 km short of the Moon
final_answer.spoken: thirty six thousand five hundred kilometres in a year, three lakh sixty five thousand kilometres in ten years, and nineteen thousand four hundred kilometres short of the Moon

names.Ruhee: the child who wonders whether travelling a hundred kilometres every day reaches the Moon in ten years

maths_rules: 3,65,000 < 3,84,400, so the Moon is not reached
the slip: 100 x 365 = 3,650, one zero instead of two
video_script.design: One idea: do a long calculation in stages, a year and then ten years, then compare with the distance. The Moon distance stays in the anchor; the working band builds each stage. Keeko's doubt: a hundred times a number adds only one zero.

A year gives thirty six thousand five hundred kilometres.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Ten years give three lakh sixty five thousand kilometres.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the traveller and the Moon
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble: 100 x 365 = 3,650; 100 x 300 = 30,000 beside it; 365 with two zeros = 36,500; the bubble crossed out
narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko thinks one hundred times three hundred sixty five is three thousand six hundred fifty.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>But one hundred times three hundred is already thirty thousand.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>A hundred puts two zeros after the number.
Three hundred sixty five with two zeros is thirty six thousand five hundred.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Two zeros, not one, so we count the zeros before we write.
